title: Should I study to work as a freelance 2D pixel artist in the context of AI?
author: Gold_Carpenter_6148
selftext:
So I'm thinking about starting to study 2D pixel art with the goal of working as a freelancer on video game projects.
I’ve always loved games, and I really enjoy staying at home. I see that these days there are many artists working this way—for indie developers or companies looking for a specific style of pixel art rather than something generic generated by AI.
But AI is getting better and better every day, and it’ll only be a matter of time (if it hasn’t already happened) before we can ask it for specific design elements, and it’ll “spit out” a model or background exactly as we wanted it—so I’d like to know what you all think? 
2D artists who work in this field, can you tell me a little about what you think regarding your professional future, current AI systems, and how AI has changed—and how you think it will continue to change—your work?

comments.author: Neathus
comments.body: 2D artists aren't going to disappear overnight. Shoemakers didn't disappear when shoes became mass-produced either. But look at the shoes you're wearing. Chances are they weren't made by a shoemaker.

replies.author: OkPrice6335
replies.body:
Aber möchtest du zum Dino werden oder direkt den Fortschrittlichen Weg perfektionieren um in Zukunft was lockerer durchzukommen? Ich würde mich komplett auf AI fokussieren. 

Was aber natürlich klar ist,  wir brauchen immer Leute die den Hintergrund raffen  falls Tech ausfällt durch irgendein Ereignis. Dann brauchen wir das wissen! Sowas müsste dann evtl. staatlich gefördert werden um am Leben zu bleiben. Aber allein um seine Brötchen zu verdienen und einfacher durchs Leben zu schlürfen, würde ich mich eher auf AI fokussieren.

replies.author: Gold_Carpenter_6148
replies.body:
I haven't had any trouble learning how to use AI in my workflow. I'm asking this because I want to know if the career I'm aiming for—being a 2D pixel artist working from home as a freelancer for video game developers—will still be possible in a couple of years, or if AI is already taking over the jobs of people in this field.

I wouldn’t mind if, instead of manually drawing the pixel art myself, my job involved learning to use the right AI tools and knowing what to tell them and how to get them to draw what I need.

That’s why I’m asking here—I want people in the industry to explain the current situation to me and share their thoughts on where they think we’re headed professionally in another 2–3 years as AI continues to improve.

replies.author: Gold_Carpenter_6148
replies.body:
So are you saying that 2D artists who are already in the field will still have work, but probably “less”? And that the field in general will have less work? 
Wouldn't it be a good idea to start learning how to create 2D pixel art characters by hand, then?

replies.author: Neathus
replies.body: The demand for manual work will decrease with time, and become more bespoke.

comments.author: DubiousTomato
comments.body:
Whether or not you should use AI comes down to your priorities. If you place a high value on quickly iterating and end results, AI is the way to go. You can get something out fairly quickly to test and build upon, and AI is good enough that most consumers wouldn't be able to tell at a glance. If you value the experience of doing something yourself and developing more than taste, learning 2D pixel art without it should be your starting point. Personally, I value the latter because you encounter more ways to learn than if you just get what you *think* you want right away. Do you have the skillset to know the difference between a good idea and a bad idea? Can you set up creative restrictions for your concept's scope that forces you to find a way around issues?  
  
You can certainly learn with AI and have it tell you about xyz concepts, but discovering those things on your own can lead your towards making choices that an AI couldn't, while solidifying it in your memory as an experience (ah-ha! moments). You can always add in AI later and have a better mental library to act with. What's your history with art? What makes you loves games and the idea of being a 2D pixel artist?

replies.author: Gold_Carpenter_6148
replies.body:
Personally, I’d start studying pixel art design on my own because of all the positive things you’ve mentioned, but I’m not asking from a love of art—I’m asking from a professional standpoint.
My goal is to learn and acquire the skills needed to work as a freelancer in character design, backgrounds, and everything related to 2D pixel art in video games.
But I want to know if the kind of work I aspire to do (as I’ve seen many people doing today) will still be in demand in another 2–3 years, considering the enormous advances in AI in recent years and how much further it has to improve.
I’d also like to know, with that goal in mind, whether it makes sense today to start by learning to create art by hand and then use AI, or to start learning directly with AI—to really understand which methods are trending, their pros and cons, how to instruct the AI to do things the way I want, etc.
There are several things that motivate me to want to learn this. First, I’m a gamer, and pixel art is one of the styles I find most beautiful; plus, the types of games that typically use this style are also my favorites.
Second, I’d like to work from home; I don’t like going out much, and I have no problem spending 10 hours a day on the computer.
I want to work as a freelancer for other developers and build an up-to-date portfolio.
I’m eager to learn, but I’m already 28—I don’t want to “waste my time” studying something only to end up working in a field that’s already become obsolete.

replies.author: DubiousTomato
replies.body:
>I want to know if the kind of work I aspire to do (as I’ve seen many people doing today) will still be in demand in another 2–3 years

I've been a designer for about 20ish years, 36. 2D pixel art will always be demanded by someone. The thing that will make people demand *you* will be your unique view on pixel art and expertise. The thing to remember is that you acquire more things than just skill in pixel art in your pursuits. If you care more about making a career, the long term is building up your own style. You might be able to immediately get commissions in a few weeks with AI, but you'll likely hit a ceiling because you won't be able to input your own feel on your work in a meaningful way. That's really the main difference, and it sounds to me like you want a larger career than something you do as a gig. Just to clarify, the only waste of time here is if you go in half-hearted. You're not too old, and it's not too late, and you can turn it into a career if you dig into it. In 2-3 years, you can build a good reputation for steady work.

comments.author: Bratchan
comments.body:
The biggest thing that will aid you is unstanding 2d pixel art.  Styling, know your pixel bits, etc. AI yes getting better etc..  But there are ALOT of flaws it does with pixels. Such it loves to blur edges. It loves to do 'squared' off section which you rarely do in outlines. It also sometimes just does a random stray Pixel of a random color.  
  
When ai gets to a point Artist jobs will be cleaning up things.. fixing things it just can't do. Even the best animations for pixels they are jumpy or it will start going back to wrong pixel shapes and so on. 

Art used to be a field just improve yourself. Its now becoming to learn 'your enemy' ai.  Which programmers we always have to learning whats knew and so on.. So now that is shifting to artist.  Understanding where AI is going to fail.. you will look at an ref and be like it will fail here and here.  Those things will help you know what your will be stuck with changing.

I have 3 characters i use even just doing base art gen. its anime style. I know it hates one of my ears i draw, its a very odd style. I been using it for a few years of AI. it has got to the point it is able to replicate the shape now, but still has issues with other points.  I have a character with 4 horns on his head, 2 are small and 2 are big. It struggles with that thought seems simple. it gotten alot better from where it started.  The last character she has a metal piece on her face and she is covered in tribal typles of tatoos. It HATES her tattoos and that metal piece. Now its at the point it can do her tats better but that metal piece it liek wha?? so makig yoru own test case you use in every version of AI that comes out will also keep your knowledge better. 

Now im programmer and an artist. I like using AI for alot of my stuff. I love doing pixel art but i alos love to see where it fails.

replies.author: Neathus
replies.body: 2D art is not something AI fundamentally can't do. Same way game dev and 3D modelling isn't. When they put more effort into training the models on these specific skills, they will improve. Look at the leap Opus 5.5 & Astra took with 3D modelling by training on data for it. Not perfect but it's going to improve rapidly. This will not age well.
